name: Limpombo head wrapping

card.summary: A traditional Mangbetu practice of wrapping infants' heads in cloth so the skull grows into an elongated shape that was admired as beautiful and a mark of status.
card.note: A historical cultural practice documented in infants; it is not presented as a method for adults.

quick.overview:
Limpombo (also spelled lipombo) is the Mangbetu tradition, from northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo, of binding a baby's head with cloth so that the soft skull gradually takes an elongated shape. The finished shape was considered attractive and a symbol of status, and it was emphasised with hairstyles and headdresses.

Because it works on an infant's still-growing skull, the shape became a lasting feature of appearance. The practice has become less common since about the 1950s, and it is documented through travellers' accounts, photographs and museum art rather than modern studies of the Mangbetu.
quick.how: Historically the binding began in infancy, reportedly about a month after birth, and was applied to girls, with the cloth kept in place while the skull was still malleable. It was paired with elaborate hairstyles that followed the elongated line of the head.
quick.risks: Descriptions of artificial cranial deformation in general list asymmetry, bleeding, infection and tissue damage in compressed areas, with the shape effects largely lost after infancy in some cases. Researchers disagree about effects on the brain, with a 2003 study reporting changes in appearance but not overall cranial size and a 2013 review proposing cognitive and neurological effects.

lead: Limpombo (Lipombo) is a traditional Mangbetu practice in which babies' heads were tightly wrapped in cloth to produce an elongated skull. The Mangbetu live in northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo.[1][3]

The elongated head was regarded as a mark of beauty and status; Discover magazine reports it was linked to attractiveness and intelligence, with binding starting about a month after birth, applied to girls.[3] Hairstyles and headdresses were designed to emphasise the shape.[1]

German botanist Georg Schweinfurth met the Mangbetu in 1870, and in the first half of the twentieth century photographers and filmmakers, including Casimir Zagourski, documented the elongated heads, royal courts and elaborate hairstyles.[1] The practice began dying out in the 1950s as Western influence spread.[1][3]

angle.text: For the Mangbetu, wrapping an infant's head produced a lasting elongated shape considered beautiful and prestigious, which was then accentuated with hairstyles.

infobox: Reportedly about one month after birth[3]

paras: Cloth was bound tightly around babies' heads, guiding skull growth while the bones were still unfused. Elongated heads were seen as a symbol of status linked to attractiveness and intelligence.[3] The general literature on artificial cranial deformation says such practices often signalled group affiliation or social status and sometimes an aesthetic preference.[2]

The Mangbetu are known for their art and music, and the elongated head shape is a recognisable feature of Mangbetu figures in African art.[1] Schweinfurth's 1874 image of King Munza dancing before his wives is one early European depiction of Mangbetu court life.[1] Early twentieth-century photographers recorded the practice.[1]
The tradition became less common after the 1950s, with sources attributing this to Belgian colonial influence and westernisation.[1][3]

General descriptions of cranial modification list strong cranial and facial asymmetry, bleeding, infection and necrosis of compressed areas as possible harms, and note that effects are partly lost after infancy as the head compensates through growth.[2] A 2003 study concluded that deformation alters facial and skull appearance without generally changing cranial size, while a 2013 review argued it significantly affected brain lobes and could cause memory, visual, motor and behavioural problems.[3] Researchers note it is hard to know how the practice affected individuals in the past.[3]
No studies found. Studies of artificial cranial deformation as a broader category exist, with differing conclusions on its effects.[3]
